subject: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
parts:
A question and a comment on normal priors in rstanarm.

1. rstanarm::normal() has a default scale = NULL. The documentation does not say what scale = NULL means, except in the specific case when it is used as the prior_intercept argument of stan_lm. In this case the stan_lm documentation says that scale is chosen to be "the marginal standard deviation of the outcome, divided by the square root of the sample size." Is that true in general?

2. The above-mentioned default scale for rstanarm::normal() is incompatible with Bayes' Rule. The problem is NOT the dependence on the sigma_Y parameter -- it is the division by sqrt(N). A legitimate prior cannot depend on the number of data points you will be observing. This default scale has you getting more and more certain of the intercept as the number of data points to be observed increases.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
parts:
On Thursday, February 25, 2016 at 10:41:12 AM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
A question and a comment on normal priors in rstanarm.

1. rstanarm::normal() has a default scale = NULL. The documentation does not say what scale = NULL means, except in the specific case when it is used as the prior_intercept argument of stan_lm. In this case the stan_lm documentation says that scale is chosen to be "the marginal standard deviation of the outcome, divided by the square root of the sample size." Is that true in general?

For models with continuous outcomes, yes. For coefficients, there is an adjustment to the prior scale based on the scales of the predictors. For other families, such as binomial, it does a 1.6 scaling of the logit priors if the model is probit but not for other link functions. I think the behavior comes from

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/priors11.pdf

2. The above-mentioned default scale for rstanarm::normal() is incompatible with Bayes' Rule. The problem is NOT the dependence on the sigma_Y parameter -- it is the division by sqrt(N). A legitimate prior cannot depend on the number of data points you will be observing. This default scale has you getting more and more certain of the intercept as the number of data points to be observed increases.

I agree that in most cases, it does not make sense to consider N to be fixed.

Ben

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
parts: On Thursday, February 25, 2016 at 10:41:12 AM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:

A question and a comment on normal priors in rstanarm.

1. rstanarm::normal() has a default scale = NULL. The documentation does not say what scale = NULL means, except in the specific case when it is used as the prior_intercept argument of stan_lm.

If you go help("priors", package = "rstanarm") then it does say the default scale is NULL because it depends on the family of prior used and whether the prior is for the intercept or for the other coefficients. For the normal prior this is the Student t family, which is described in a section in the same help page: 

If scale is not specified it will default to 10 for the intercept and 2.5 for the other coefficients, unless the probit link function is used, in which case these defaults are scaled by a factor of dnorm(0)/dlogis(0), which is roughly 1.6.

I don't believe we do any scaling by 1/sqrt(N) for stan_glm or stan_glmer. Regarding the particular case of stan_lm, Ben would know best.
